queue.li_title: DSCR Cash-Out Refinance Seasoning: 3, 6, and 12 Months
queue.li_desc: Why seasoning windows exist, what they cost investors, and what each window really costs a BRRRR investor.
queue.li:
The number that decides how fast a BRRRR investor scales isn't the rehab budget or the ARV. It's the seasoning window.

Most DSCR lenders require 6-12 months of ownership before a cash-out refinance can use the new appraised value. That's 6-12 months of your capital parked in a finished, rented property doing nothing.

Our window is 3 months. No lease required at closing — the market-rent appraisal qualifies.

On a $110K cash-in deal, getting your capital back at month 3 instead of month 6 is the difference between four cycles a year and two. At portfolio scale, that compounds into an entirely different growth curve.

The full math, including the delayed-financing exception: https://slacapital.ai/blog/dscr-cash-out-seasoning/

queue.li_title: Hard Money vs. DSCR Loans: Which One Fits Your Deal?
queue.li_desc: Two tools, two jobs — and the bridge-to-DSCR play that combines them.
queue.li:
Investors ask us which is better — hard money or DSCR. Wrong question. They're different tools for different jobs, and the best operators use both on the same property.

Hard money buys the project: 6-24 months, interest-only, sized off after-repair value, funds the rehab, closes in as little as 72 hours.

DSCR holds the property: 30-year term from 6.90%, qualified on the rent it produces — no tax returns, no DTI.

The combined play is the standard BRRRR sequence: acquire and renovate on bridge, stabilize, refinance into DSCR at month 3, recycle the capital. One lender across both loans means the second underwrite starts warm instead of from scratch.

Full comparison: https://slacapital.ai/blog/hard-money-vs-dscr-loans/

queue.li_title: Portfolio Loans for Rental Properties: One Note for 2–10 Rentals
queue.li_desc: How blanket loans qualify on combined rent, why the release clause decides your flexibility later, and when separate loans still win.
queue.li:
Somewhere around rental number five, the debt stack turns into a second job. Five loans, five payments, five insurance renewals, five lender portals.

The portfolio loan is the fix. One 30-year DSCR note secured by 2 to 10 rentals at once, qualified on combined market rent against combined PITIA. A strong property can carry a slightly weaker one inside the blanket, which is the quiet advantage over financing each door alone, where the weakest property gets declined on its own merits.

What actually improves:

Administration collapses. One payment, one escrow account, one renewal calendar. At eight doors that is hours a month back.

Closing costs collapse. One title order and one closing instead of eight, and the savings scale with the property count.

Equity works as a team. Aggregate loan-to-value is what gets underwritten, so a low-leverage property lets the pool support more than door-by-door caps would allow.

The clause that decides everything is the release. Before signing any blanket loan, know three numbers for every property in it: the allocated balance, the release price, and whether releases are capped per year. A portfolio loan with clean release terms is flexible. One without them is a roach motel.

And the honest counterargument. If you are about to sell several properties, separate loans exit cleaner. If one property is your crown jewel with outsized equity, blanketing it ties it up to subsidize the pool. Two properties barely justify the structure. The sweet spot starts around four.

Send the address list and the rents and the term sheet will show the whole pool priced as one.

queue.theme: DSCR requirements / no tax returns is not no requirements
queue.li_title: DSCR Loan Requirements: Credit, Down Payment, Reserves & Property Types
queue.li_desc: The checklist a DSCR underwriter actually works through, where the flexible lanes are, and the four things you will never be asked for.
queue.li:
The pitch on DSCR loans is that the property qualifies, not you. That part is true. It also gets misheard as no requirements at all, and that misunderstanding is what costs investors a closing.

Here is the checklist an underwriter actually works:

The ratio. Monthly rent divided by monthly PITIA, meaning principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and association dues. Most lenders want 1.0 to 1.2 or better for standard pricing, and a below-1.0 lane exists at adjusted terms for strong deals in appreciating markets. Rent comes from the lease in place, or from the appraiser’s market rent report if the property is vacant. No active lease is required at closing.

Credit. The practical floor is a 660 mid FICO, with meaningful pricing tiers at roughly 680, 700, 720, and 740 and above. If you sit a few points under a tier and a card payoff is about to post, waiting a month can genuinely pay.

Leverage. Purchases and rate-and-term refinances go up to 80% loan-to-value, cash-out up to 75%. Caps step down for lower credit tiers, lower ratios, and less common property types. An advertised maximum is the ceiling for a clean file, not a promise for every file.

Reserves. Three to six months of PITIA in liquid funds after closing, scaling with portfolio size. The eighth property draws more cushion than the first.

Property type. Single-family, 2 to 4 units, and warrantable condos are the core box. Short-term rentals, rural properties, mixed-use, and unique builds need a conversation rather than a rate sheet.

And the four things you will not be asked for: tax returns, employment verification, a personal debt-to-income calculation, and a cap on how many financed properties you already own. DSCR lenders never inherited the 10-property limit.

Loans run from $100K to $3M across 42 states, closed in your entity. The full breakdown is here.
